# Implementation Plan: Python Library-Based UI

**Branch**: `002-python-library-ui` | **Date**: October 17, 2025 | **Spec**: [spec.md](./spec.md)  
**Input**: Feature specification from `/specs/002-python-library-ui/spec.md`

**Note**: This plan was generated by the `/speckit.plan` command using NiceGUI as the chosen UI framework.

## Summary

**Primary Requirement**: Add a modern Python web-based visual interface to the Pomodoro Timer application, allowing users to see timer countdown, control sessions via buttons, view session history, and configure durations.

**Technical Approach**: Use NiceGUI as the UI framework - a modern, reactive Python library that runs as a local web server. NiceGUI provides built-in `ui.timer` for real-time countdown display, full async/await support for integration with the existing `TimerEngine`, and excellent testing capabilities via the `user` fixture. The UI is implemented as a presentation layer that observes and controls the existing timer engine without duplicating business logic. Session history persisted in SQLite, configuration stored in TOML format.

## Technical Context

**Language/Version**: Python 3.12+  
**Primary Dependencies**: 
- NiceGUI (modern reactive web UI framework)
- tomli-w (TOML writing, stdlib tomllib for reading)
- Existing: asyncio, sqlite3 (stdlib)

**Storage**: 
- SQLite database (`~/.local/share/pomodoro-timer/sessions.db`) for session history
- TOML file (`~/.config/pomodoro-timer/config.toml`) for user settings

**Testing**: pytest with NiceGUI plugin (`nicegui.testing.user_plugin` for fast Python-level UI tests)

**Target Platform**: Local machine (Windows/Linux/macOS), runs as localhost web server, browser-based UI

**Project Type**: Single project (adding UI module to existing CLI application)

**Performance Goals**: 
- UI startup <2 seconds
- Timer display updates <500ms latency
- Support 10,000+ session history records without performance degradation

**Constraints**: 
- Real-time updates (1-second intervals for countdown)
- Responsive UI at 800x600 minimum window size
- Single-user, local-only (no cloud/multi-user requirements)
- Must integrate with existing `TimerEngine` without duplicating countdown logic

**Scale/Scope**: 
- Single user application
- ~5 UI screens/views (main timer, history, settings)
- ~10 UI components (timer display, buttons, history table, settings form, etc.)
- Expected <1,000 lines of UI code (excluding tests)

## Constitution Check

*GATE: Must pass before Phase 0 research. Re-check after Phase 1 design.*

Verify alignment with Pomodoro Timer Constitution (`.specify/memory/constitution.md`):

- [x] **Principle I (Test-First)**: Feature has testable acceptance criteria in spec.md ✅ All user stories have Given/When/Then scenarios. Will write tests first using NiceGUI `user` fixture.
- [x] **Principle II (Type Safety & Quality)**: Plan includes type hints, docstrings, and quality gates ✅ All code will have type hints (enforced by ty), Google docstrings (enforced by ruff), and pass quality checks before commit.
- [x] **Principle III (Incremental)**: Feature broken into independent, prioritized user stories (P1, P2, P3) ✅ P1 (timer display + controls), P2 (session history), P3 (settings) - each independently testable and deliverable.
- [x] **Principle IV (Modern Tooling)**: Uses uv/ruff/ty/pytest ✅ No manual pyproject.toml edits, using `uv add` for dependencies. Existing tooling chain maintained.
- [x] **Principle V (Simplicity)**: No premature abstractions ✅ UI is thin presentation layer over existing engine. See justification below for NiceGUI framework addition.

**Violations** (must be justified in Complexity Tracking section if checked):
- [x] Adding dependency when stdlib could work
- [ ] Creating abstraction before 3rd repetition
- [ ] Framework introduction without clear need
- [ ] Skipping tests or implementing before test approval

**Justification for NiceGUI Dependency** (see Complexity Tracking below):
- User explicitly requested "python library based ui" and specified "nicegui"
- Standard library has no web UI framework (tkinter is desktop-only, doesn't meet "modern web UI" requirement)
- Requirement FR-014 explicitly mandates integration with existing timer engine without duplication - requires separate UI layer
- NiceGUI is lightweight, Pythonic, and has excellent testing support (aligns with Principle I)
- Alternative approaches (Flask+React, Streamlit) are either too complex or incompatible with stateful timer requirements

**Structure Decision**: This is **Option 1: Single project** - we are adding a UI module to the existing CLI application, not creating a separate web app or mobile app. The UI module (`src/pomodoro_timer/ui/`) is a sibling to the existing `cli/` module, with both using the shared `models/` and `timer/` modules. This maintains clean separation while allowing code reuse.

**Rationale**:
- UI and CLI share the same timer engine and session models (DRY principle)
- Users can choose interface mode via command-line flag (`pomodoro-timer --ui` vs. `pomodoro-timer`)
- Single codebase simplifies development, testing, and deployment
- No need for separate backend/frontend or API layer (local application)
- Aligns with "simple python library based ui" requirement

## Complexity Tracking

*Filled because Constitution Check has one justified violation*

| Violation | Why Needed | Simpler Alternative Rejected Because |
|-----------|------------|-------------------------------------|
| Adding NiceGUI framework dependency | User explicitly requested "python library based ui" and specified "nicegui". Requirement FR-014 mandates integration with existing timer engine without duplication - requires separate UI layer. No standard library solution exists for modern web UIs (tkinter is desktop-only, outdated, and doesn't meet "modern web UI" requirement). | **Tkinter** (stdlib): Outdated appearance, poor async support, difficult to test, no web deployment option. **Streamlit**: Incompatible execution model (full script rerun on interaction) cannot maintain persistent timer state. **Flask+React**: Requires JavaScript development and build tooling, violates "simple python library" requirement, far too complex for a timer UI. **No UI**: Does not fulfill the feature requirement which is literally to add a visual interface. |

**Conclusion**: The NiceGUI framework is the minimal complexity solution that meets all requirements. It is:
- Pure Python (no JavaScript required)
- Modern and reactive (meets "most modern python web ui" requirement)
- Lightweight (single dependency, <10MB)
- Excellent async support (integrates seamlessly with existing TimerEngine)
- Superior testing story (fast Python-level tests via `user` fixture)
- Backed by active development and good documentation

This is not premature complexity - it is the necessary and appropriate tool for the stated requirement.
